title: No work, no food
hook: the Chan master Baizhang: a day without work is a day without food (Chan tradition)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha's short list of trades to leave alone. Your line was harm into the hands of someone else. When you asked whether your work harms, what did you find? Today, a teacher who wouldn't stop working. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `HARM INTO THE HANDS OF SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: The tools are gone. The hoe, the rake, whatever he used in the fields, hidden somewhere by his own students. They meant well. Their teacher was old, the Chan tradition says, and still went out every day to work the land beside the monks, and they wanted him to rest. So they hid his tools. He didn't argue. He didn't search. He just didn't eat that day. When they asked him why, the answer has been passed down in Chan and Zen communities: a day without work is a day without food. The teacher was Baizhang. Today's word is the first half of his saying.
screen: `THE TOOLS ARE HIDDEN.` → `HE DOESN'T EAT.` → `A DAY WITHOUT WORK.`

segments.voice: First, who Baizhang is in the story. Chan is the Chinese school of Buddhism known in Japan as Zen. Tradition remembers Baizhang as a Chan master who shaped how a Chan monastery ran day to day: when to sit, when to eat, and when to work. In this telling, the monks didn't only meditate. They farmed, cooked, swept and hauled, and the teacher worked with them. Second, what the saying is not. It's easy to hear no work, no food as a threat, the kind a boss might shout. But in the story, Baizhang says it of himself. Nobody punishes him. He simply keeps his own rule. The sharpness is aimed inward. Third, a difference worth saying plainly. In other Buddhist communities, monks live on alms, food given by lay people, and that giving is itself a practice for the givers. The Chan way of working the land grew up alongside that, as a different arrangement, not a correction of it. Both are ways of keeping a community fed and a mind awake. Fourth, what it might mean at a kitchen table. In a monastery, work is shared. Nobody's job is beneath anyone. Somebody washes the pots, and the teacher might be the one with his sleeves rolled up. At home, the same question waits by the sink. Who does the dishes? Who takes out the trash? Baizhang's saying doesn't ask you to earn your dinner in money. It asks whether you've done your share of what keeps the place running.
screen: `A CHAN MASTER IN THE FIELDS.` · `A RULE HE KEPT FOR HIMSELF.` · `ALMS, OR THE HOE: BOTH FEED.` · `YOUR SHARE AT HOME.` · then, large: `NO WORK, NO FOOD.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle and the breath slow down. Baizhang's rule pointed at himself, not at the monks. Try that turn. Think of one thing you wish other people at home would do. Rinse the cup. Close the cupboard. Put the shoes away. Notice the small heat of that wish, without scolding it. Now turn it around, the way he did. Make it a rule for you alone, just for today, and tell nobody. Hold the rule quietly while the breath comes and goes. If you pray, you can bring your household into it, in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
No work. The first half of Baizhang's saying, a day without work is a day without food: a rule he kept for himself. Today's word.
Your line: sleeves rolled up. Today, before dinner, do your share of the chores, and maybe one more. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries, monks and teachers share manual work such as cooking, cleaning and gardening as part of daily practice, and Baizhang's saying is often quoted about it.

fork.setup: you're Baizhang. you're old, and your students have hidden your tools so you'll rest. what do you do?
options: thank them and take the day off.
search the monastery until you find them.
fork.reveal: the tradition says he simply didn't eat, and explained: a day without work is a day without food. a rule kept for himself, not for them.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strict boss's rule. no work, no dinner.
what it means: a Chan teacher's rule for himself, so that the shared work of the community was shared by him too.
what a scholar hears: Baizhang, remembered as shaping the daily order of Chan monasteries, working the land alongside the older practice of living on alms.
recall: your own dharma, your own duty

notes: The hidden-tools story and the saying are told as Chan tradition, not as documented fact. A Buddhist Keeper should confirm the framing and name the classical source (e.g. later Chan records) if wanted.

'Tradition remembers Baizhang as a Chan master who shaped how a Chan monastery ran' refers to the monastic rules traditionally credited to him; their authorship is debated by historians. Confirm phrasing.

'In other Buddhist communities, monks live on alms' is a general description not stated by a cited text; a Keeper should confirm it. 'Chan ... later traveled to Japan as Zen' is likewise uncited general history; confirm.
Chinese 一日不作，一日不食 and pinyin yi ri bu zuo, yi ri bu shi: confirm characters and the pronunciation guide.
Alms and field work are presented as two arrangements, neither ranked.
Editor: softened the uncited history line about Chan traveling to Japan to 'known in Japan as Zen'.

Audit: the practice (notice who does the household jobs and take one someone else carries) repeated day 889's practice almost exactly; replaced with turning a rule you wish others kept into a quiet rule for yourself, which follows the teach's point that Baizhang aimed the saying inward.
